items.summary: Weston called Blake one of his “regular guys”, the bassist of his trio on “Zep Tepi”, and named him on “Saga”, “Khepera”, the 1997 Montreal residency, the Brooklyn church concert, St. Lucia, and as the one he took to the Kamigamo Shinto shrine.

items.his_quote: I had my regular guys: Alex Blake and Neil Clark.

more_his_quotes.quote: I played at the Shinto shrine last year, and this time I took Alex Blake.
I think we had Victor Lewis on drums, Alex Blake on bass, Benny Powell, you know.
I had Neil Clarke, Alex Blake; you had Billy Harper, T.K. Blue, and Benny Powell.

items.name: Alex Blake

items.summary: Weston named Powell in his band on “Saga”, “Khepera”, Montreal, the Brooklyn church concert and St. Lucia, and recalled him crying “We have adventure!” as the sextet rode donkeys up to Jajouka — echoing the line Jenkins quoted from Powell, his trombonist of many years.
items.one_liner: trombonist; cried “we have adventure!” on the donkeys
items.his_quote: Benny said, “We have adventure! We have adventure!”

more_his_quotes.quote: I had Neil Clarke, Alex Blake; you had Billy Harper, T.K. Blue, and Benny Powell.
Eric Asante, African percussion from Ghana I had Benny Powell, and I had Billy Hopper.
With all that music, with ourselves, I had TK Blue, Benny Powell, Alex Blake, Neil Clarke with the six Gnawa, and the night before that we had Olatunji.
I think we had Victor Lewis on drums, Alex Blake on bass, Benny Powell, you know.

items.notes: The 'Benny' in 309859 (St. Lucia quintet) and 309887 (Jajouka) is Benny Powell, but the pipeline folded the surface 'Benny' into Benny Bailey (109397). Instrument 'trombone' comes from Jenkins (309883: 'Your trombone player, Benny Powell…'). Upstream 'collaborated with' undersells a standing band membership.

items.summary: Weston named Harper on “Saga”, the jazz night at Montreal in 1997 and the 1972 Tangier festival, and recalled that on the trip to Jajouka he was the only one who stayed cool because, being from Texas, he could ride donkeys.

items.his_quote: Billy Harper was the only one that was cool, because Billy, being from Texas, he knew how to ride horses and donkeys.

more_his_quotes.quote: I had Neil Clarke, Alex Blake; you had Billy Harper, T.K. Blue, and Benny Powell.
The next night was like, kind of like, jazz. I had Billy Harper and Walter Rodney…
Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
Eric Asante, African percussion from Ghana I had Benny Powell, and I had Billy Hopper.

items.notes: 'Billy Hopper' (309885, sextet roll-call for the Morocco film) is Billy Harper: 309887 then says 'Billy Harper was the only one that was cool'. In 1972 he came as part of 'Max Roach’s without Max'. Instrument (tenor sax) not stated.

items.summary: Weston said he was very close to Duke, played a seven-minute solo tribute to him at Montreal in 1974, the year Ellington died, and described Ellington as having passed him the baton like a relay race.
items.one_liner: “very close to duke”; passed him the baton
items.his_quote: That’s something that I’ll always be excited about, and I’ll always be humble and grateful that I’ve been given a gift and to be able to, like a relay race, Mr. Ellington me passed the baton to me.

more_his_quotes.quote: That was the year that Duke Ellington died. I was very close to Duke and I did a solo rendition of Duke Ellington, just solo piano, about seven minutes.
I looked at Duke Ellington, like this, sitting in front of him.
I used to say, “Why did Duke Ellington play those same songs all the time? He’s got about 10,000 compositions.
What Louie Armstrong and Buddy Boland, and Duke Ellington, all they created, that’s our royalty going back to Africa itself.

items.notes: 'Very close to Duke' is the only personal-tie statement; the stronger theme is influence/lineage ('following Mr. Ellington', the baton). The baton sentence is garbled ('Mr. Ellington me passed the baton to me. Mr. Ellington said to Gillespie, “He passed it on me.') Weston also mentions Duke’s sister Ruth Ellington (other chunk).
items.name: Duke Ellington

items.summary: Weston said he plays the piano the way he does because he had human contact with Thelonious Monk, whom he counted among the royalty of piano he grew up with.
items.one_liner: the human contact that shaped his piano
items.his_quote: I play the piano like I play because I had the human contact with Thelonious Monk, because I had the spiritual contact with Nat King Cole, who I never met.

more_his_quotes.quote: But following Mr. Ellington, following Mr. Thelonious Monk, many of the musicians of the 20’s and the 30’s and 40’s, they wrote music about their families.

When you grow up with people like Dorothy Dandridge and Duke Ellington, and Count Basie, and Art Tatum, Earl Hines, Nat King Cole, Monk, I mean, you know that period, for me, it was the royalty of piano.

items.notes: Upstream 'has met' is true but undersells it; Weston states the contact shaped how he plays. Jenkins also mentions 'the Monk book' by Robin Kelley (309881).
items.name: Thelonious Monk

items.summary: Weston said he met Bernstein during his summers in the Berkshires near the Boston Symphony Orchestra and spoke of “my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas”, the seven waltzes for children that began with “Earth Birth”.
items.one_liner: met in the berkshires summers
items.his_quote: I met people like Luckas Foss and Leonard Bernstein.

more_his_quotes.quote: So, my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas, it was called seven waltzes for children.

items.notes: 'Has met' is certain. 'Collaborated with' rests only on the phrase 'my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas', which may be garbled or loose (no such joint recording is known); a human should decide between collaborated with and has met.
items.name: Leonard Bernstein

items.identity_note: Transcript has 'Luckas Foss' and, a few sentences later, 'Lucas'; read as Lukas Foss, the composer-conductor active at Tanglewood/the Boston Symphony in the Berkshires.
items.summary: Weston said he met Foss in the Berkshires through the Boston Symphony Orchestra milieu and spoke of “my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas”, the waltzes for children.
items.one_liner: met in the berkshires summers
items.his_quote: I met people like Luckas Foss and Leonard Bernstein.

more_his_quotes.quote: So, my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas, it was called seven waltzes for children.

items.notes: Same doubt as Bernstein: 'has met' is certain, the joint recording is only the one loose phrase. 'Lucas' in the same block is Foss, not Clyde Lucas.
items.name: Lukas Foss

items.summary: Weston said only Melba Liston could arrange “Spirit of Our Ancestors”, told how he goaded her back to work after her stroke — she learned to write music on a computer with her left hand — and recalled her arrangements arriving from a California hospital in time for the 1959 Five Spot date and the 1985 Montreal concert.
items.one_liner: his arranger; wrote left-handed after her stroke
items.his_quote: I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know?

more_his_quotes.quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
Well, it was her genius and her strength, and her spiritual strength.
Spirit. It makes no difference where she was: North Pole, or the middle of the Congo, it makes no difference.
She was in the hospital in California, and by some miracle the music arrived the day of the recording.

items.notes: Jenkins supplies 'such a long partnership'. Weston says Melba 'can no longer play the trombone'.
items.name: Melba Liston

more_his_quotes.quote: You know, and he’s older than Johnny Copeland, which I found out.

items.notes: 'Normally we would have' implies earlier collaboration (the “Volcano” album); the transcript does not say more.

items.summary: Weston could not recall the name — Jenkins supplied “Robert Lockwood Jr.” and Weston agreed — but described the older bluesman who sang the 1997 Montreal blues night, doubted the band at first and was very happy after rehearsal.
items.one_liner: the older bluesman on the montreal blues night
items.his_quote: He sang, and at first I got the feeling he didn’t quite know we could play the blues, you know. But, after rehearsal he was very happy, and then I found out later on he was into jazz before and the blues.

more_his_quotes.quote: So, we got this older brother, his name escapes me now…
You know, and he’s older than Johnny Copeland, which I found out.

items.notes: Name rests on Jenkins (309825 'Robert Lockwood Jr.') and Weston's 'Exactly.' (309826); everything else is Weston's. Lockwood was a guitarist; the transcript only says 'He sang'.

items.summary: Weston called Coleman Hawkins his idol — at 17 he bought three copies of “Body and Soul” and hid two — and said recording with him live at the Five Spot in 1959 was another miracle.
items.one_liner: his idol; on his 1959 five spot date

more_his_quotes.quote: So, for the recordings, I think it was 1959 at the Five Spot, a live date.
When Coleman Hawkins picks up his saxophone he only has to hit one note, you see?
I had the spiritual contact with Count Basie, or Coleman Hawkins, or Dizzy Gillespie. I saw them, I touched their hands, you see?
